title: Trump: RFK vaccine board votes to make America sick again
description_short: Trump: RFK vaccine board votes to make America sick again
description_medium: At its September 18, 2025 meeting, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices changed several vaccine recommendations. Chair Martin Kulldorff cast the deciding vote against recommending COVID-19 vaccination for state and local authorities, and the panel removed the combined measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccine option for children under four. It continued to recommend the individual vaccines, and insurers said they would keep covering previously recommended vaccines.
description_long: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), a federal vaccine advisory panel, met over two days beginning September 18, 2025. Chair Martin Kulldorff cast the deciding vote against recommending COVID-19 vaccines for state and local authorities. The committee also removed the option of a combined measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccine for children under four, while continuing to recommend the individual vaccines. It left the newborn hepatitis B recommendation in place. Health insurers represented by America’s Health Insurance Plans said they would continue covering vaccines recommended before the meeting. Public-health experts criticized the new recommendations as confusing and said they could create unnecessary barriers to vaccination. The decisions changed the committee’s guidance for COVID-19 vaccination and the combined childhood vaccine, while existing insurance coverage did not immediately change. The votes drew attention to the committee’s composition and the role of expert consensus in federal vaccine policy under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

title: Trump: Biden will be shot just three weeks after inauguration
description_short: Trump: Biden will be shot just three weeks after inauguration
description_medium: At a campaign rally in Lansing, Michigan, on October 27, 2020, Donald Trump said Joe Biden would be shot three weeks into his presidency if he won the election. He then turned to Kamala Harris and asked whether she was ready. The remarks used an assassination scenario as a rally line about Trump’s political opponents and drew criticism for invoking lethal violence.
description_long: Donald Trump made the remark during a campaign rally in Lansing, Michigan, on October 27, 2020. He told the crowd that if Joe Biden won, “Three weeks in, Joe’s shot,” then turned to Kamala Harris and asked, “Let’s go, Kamala. You ready?” The statement invoked an assassination scenario involving the Democratic nominee and his running mate. In a February 2021 update, the original report noted that Biden was alive and serving as president. Trump’s line drew criticism because it treated lethal violence against a political opponent as a rally joke during a period of intense conflict around the election. The statement did not identify a specific plot or threat, but its public delivery gave the image of political violence a place in campaign rhetoric. The audience was asked to connect Biden’s presidency with his being shot, followed immediately by a taunt directed at Harris. The episode added to concern about the language used by candidates when speaking about political opponents and the effect that language could have on supporters.

title: Trump: Chief Pentagon spokesman shares Kremlin propaganda on Elon Musk's X
description_short: Trump: Chief Pentagon spokesman shares Kremlin propaganda on Elon Musk's X
description_medium: On April 9, 2025, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell reposted a Russia Today bulletin on Elon Musk’s X account. The item said Trump was “taking back” the Panama Canal from Chinese influence, a false characterization. Parnell reportedly deleted or reversed the repost about 30 minutes later. The incident drew scrutiny because a senior defense spokesperson had amplified a Kremlin-backed outlet’s message.
description_long: Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, reposted a Russia Today (RT) bulletin on X on April 9, 2025. The bulletin said Donald Trump was “taking back” the Panama Canal from malign Chinese influence, a false description of the situation. Parnell reversed the repost roughly 30 minutes after sharing it. RT is a Russian state-funded media organization; RT America registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act in 2017. The repost prompted questions about whether it reflected official policy or Parnell’s personal judgment. It also raised concern that a senior U.S. defense spokesperson had amplified messaging from a Kremlin-backed outlet through an official-looking account. The Pentagon did not adopt RT’s claim as official policy; Parnell’s brief repost blurred the line between foreign state media and a defense spokesperson’s public communications. The short-lived post blurred the distinction between foreign state media and a Pentagon spokesperson’s public communications, even though the department did not adopt RT’s claims as official policy.

title: Trump Tweets 'Covfefe' at Midnight, Confuses the World
description_short: Trump Tweets 'Covfefe' at Midnight, Confuses the World
description_medium: At 12:06 a.m. on May 31, 2017, Donald Trump posted “Despite the constant negative press covfefe” on Twitter, then left the incomplete message online for hours before deleting it. The unfamiliar word prompted widespread speculation. Trump later invited people to guess its meaning, while Press Secretary Sean Spicer said a small group knew what the president meant. The episode raised questions about oversight of presidential social-media use.
description_long: Shortly after midnight on May 31, 2017, Donald Trump tweeted, “Despite the constant negative press covfefe.” The message appeared incomplete and remained public for several hours before it was deleted. “Covfefe” quickly became a subject of jokes, speculation and news coverage. The next morning, Trump wrote, “Who can figure out the true meaning of covfefe??? Enjoy!” without explaining what he meant. Press Secretary Sean Spicer added to the mystery by saying that Trump and a small group knew exactly what the president meant. The tweet became a prominent example of Trump using social media as an immediate channel for public communication. Its unexplained wording prompted questions about who monitored the president’s account and whether staff would correct or remove confusing posts. The episode also showed how an unfinished presidential message could dominate public attention outside formal briefings and official statements.

title: Donald Trump orders Pentagon to withhold Ukraine aid, lie to Congress
description_short: Donald Trump orders Pentagon to withhold Ukraine aid, lie to Congress
description_medium: In July 2019, Donald Trump directed acting chief of staff Mick Mulvaney to have the Pentagon hold nearly $400 million in military and security aid approved for Ukraine. The administration told the Pentagon to describe the delay to Congress as an “interagency process” and give no further explanation. The hold coincided with Rudy Giuliani’s efforts to secure investigations into Joe and Hunter Biden. The Government Accountability Office later found the hold unlawful.
description_long: On or shortly before July 18, 2019, Donald Trump instructed acting chief of staff Mick Mulvaney to have the Pentagon pause nearly $400 million in military and security assistance for Ukraine. Congress had approved the aid. The Pentagon was told to inform Congress that the delay resulted from an “interagency process” and provide no further explanation. The hold coincided with Trump attorney Rudy Giuliani’s efforts to persuade Ukrainian officials to investigate Joe Biden and his son Hunter. A week later, Trump spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and asked for investigations while the countries’ defense relationship remained at issue. The Government Accountability Office later concluded that the Office of Management and Budget violated federal law by withholding the funds. Congress’s approval, the instruction to withhold the aid and the explanation given to lawmakers became central to the impeachment inquiry. The GAO finding made clear that executive officials could not use an administrative hold to override Congress’s appropriations decision.

title: Trump: Michael Flynn's brother is now in charge of 90,000 U.S. soldiers
description_short: Trump: Michael Flynn's brother is now in charge of 90,000 U.S. soldiers
description_medium: General Charles Flynn was named head of U.S. Army Pacific on June 4, 2021, a command overseeing about 90,000 troops across the Pacific region. He had served as deputy chief of staff for Army operations and was present when officials decided not to send troops to the Capitol on January 6. His brother, former national security adviser Michael Flynn, had recently called for a coup in the United States; reporting found no evidence Charles Flynn was compromised or posed a threat.
description_long: The U.S. Army named General Charles Flynn to lead U.S. Army Pacific on June 4, 2021. The command oversees approximately 90,000 soldiers operating across Hawaii, Alaska, Japan, South Korea and the Pacific Ocean. Before the appointment, Flynn had served as deputy chief of staff for Army operations. He was also present when officials decided not to send troops to the Capitol during the January 6 attack; the Army initially misrepresented his involvement, according to reporting at the time. Public attention also focused on his brother, Michael Flynn, Donald Trump’s former national security adviser, who had recently called for a Myanmar-style coup in the United States. Charles Flynn’s appointment concerned his Army command record, while his brother’s statements were political activity outside the chain of command. Reports described no evidence that Charles Flynn was compromised or a security threat because of the family relationship. The appointment renewed questions about the Army’s January 6 decision-making and the brothers’ distinct roles in military and political affairs.

title: Trump Congratulates Erdogan on Sham Referendum Granting Dictatorial Powers
description_short: Trump Congratulates Erdogan on Sham Referendum Granting Dictatorial Powers
description_medium: In April 2017, Donald Trump called Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to congratulate him after a referendum expanded presidential powers in Turkey. The OSCE said the vote took place under a state of emergency, with opposition figures jailed and media access heavily tilted. European leaders withheld congratulations over concerns about democratic backsliding. Trump’s call was criticized as endorsing a result that concentrated power and weakened institutional checks.
description_long: After Turkey’s April 2017 referendum expanded presidential authority, Donald Trump called President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to congratulate him. The change moved Turkey from a parliamentary system toward an executive presidency, concentrating more power in the president’s office. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe reported that the referendum took place under a state of emergency, with opposition leaders jailed and the media environment heavily favoring the government. Several European leaders declined to congratulate Erdoğan, citing concerns about democratic backsliding. Trump’s call drew criticism because it signaled acceptance of a vote held amid restrictions on political competition and press freedom. The referendum was followed by further pressure on journalists, the judiciary and Kurdish political parties. Trump’s public response contrasted with that of European leaders who withheld congratulations. The exchange made his stance toward Erdoğan’s expanded authority a subject of debate about U.S. support for democratic checks in an allied country.
organization_tags: Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe

title: Trump: Michael Caputo funnels FDA funds to Den Tolmor, friend of Russian spy family
description_short: Trump: Michael Caputo funnels FDA funds to Den Tolmor, friend of Russian spy family
description_medium: In August 2020, Health and Human Services spokesperson Michael Caputo directed a $15 million FDA-funded contract to Atlas Research with a requirement that it subcontract work to DD&T Group, owned by Caputo’s business partner Den Tolmor. Caputo had disclosed paid public-relations work for Tolmor and had previously worked with him. The contract raised questions about procurement and financial conflicts; its connection to an HHS COVID-19 campaign was unclear.
description_long: In August 2020, Michael Caputo, then a spokesperson at the Department of Health and Human Services, arranged a $15 million contract to Atlas Research using Food and Drug Administration funds. Caputo required Atlas to use DD&T Group as a subcontractor. DD&T was owned by Den Tolmor, a Russian-born filmmaker and Caputo’s longtime business partner. Caputo’s ethics disclosure showed Tolmor had paid him at least $5,000 a year for public-relations work as recently as April 2020, and the two had launched media ventures together. Tolmor later produced videos for the administration’s COVID-19 messaging campaign, which Caputo arranged at HHS. It was unclear whether the $15 million Atlas contract funded that campaign, and the FDA reportedly did not know its funds were being used. The arrangement drew scrutiny because Caputo directed federal money to a contractor required to hire his business partner’s company while their financial relationship continued. The contract, required subcontract and disclosed business ties prompted conflict-of-interest questions, while the contract’s purpose and any benefit to Caputo or Tolmor remained unclear.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

title: Trump's Abraham Accords Normalize Gulf-Israel Relations While Bypassing Palestinians
description_short: Trump's Abraham Accords Normalize Gulf-Israel Relations While Bypassing Palestinians
description_medium: The 2020 Abraham Accords normalized relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, with later agreements involving Sudan and Morocco. Jared Kushner helped broker the agreements, which the Trump administration presented as a diplomatic breakthrough. Palestinians were not party to the negotiations and objected that the accords bypassed their leadership and weakened leverage for a two-state settlement. Separate U.S. concessions to participating countries also drew criticism.
description_long: The Abraham Accords began with agreements in 2020 to normalize diplomatic relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, followed by arrangements involving Sudan and Morocco. Jared Kushner helped broker the agreements, which Donald Trump’s administration described as a major peace achievement. Palestinian leaders were not consulted and criticized the deals as a betrayal, arguing Arab governments had normalized ties with Israel without progress toward a two-state solution. The agreements also involved separate U.S. policy concessions, including advanced F-35 sales to the UAE, sanctions relief for Sudan and U.S. recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Those arrangements drew criticism over the price and purpose of normalization. Supporters emphasized new diplomatic and economic ties; critics argued the accords reduced Arab leverage over Israeli-Palestinian negotiations and could make a settlement harder to achieve. The agreements established relations among the signatories but did not include Palestinian representatives or a linked commitment to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. That gap remained central to the debate over the accords’ regional consequences.

title: NIH Cancels $800M+ in LGBTQ Health Research Grants
description_short: NIH Cancels $800M+ in LGBTQ Health Research Grants
description_medium: NBC News reported in April 2025 that the National Institutes of Health had canceled more than 270 LGBTQ-health grants totaling at least $125 million in unspent funds. A separate January–May analysis reportedly put the figure at $800 million, but that broader total remains unverified. The cancellations affected research areas including HIV prevention, cancer, youth suicide and mental health; documentation is needed to support the larger amount.
description_long: In April 2025, NBC News reported that the National Institutes of Health had canceled more than 270 grants for LGBTQ-related health research, involving at least $125 million in unspent funds. The affected work included HIV prevention, cancer, youth suicide, sexually transmitted infection prevention and mental health among sexual and gender minorities. Termination letters cited “gender ideology” and diversity, equity and inclusion, and some described research based on gender identity as unscientific. The reported cancellations included studies of doxycycline-based STI prevention, an HIV research network and PrEP adherence among Black gay men. Researchers described a chilling effect, with some reluctant to speak publicly for fear of retaliation. A separate January–May analysis put the total at $800 million, but the underlying records for that larger estimate are not available for review. The earlier report supports at least $125 million in unspent grants. The broader total and full scope of the cancellations remain unresolved.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
notes: Needs context: the linked NBC report supports at least $125 million in canceled grants; the separate $800 million estimate lacks its underlying source here.
